name: Mould-starter (qu) fermentation in Early Neolithic north China
summary: Early Neolithic villagers in the Wei River valley of north China fermented cereal drinks with mouldy-grain starters, the earliest known evidence of the method behind East Asian brewing.
description: Residues inside pottery from Guantaoyuan, an Early Neolithic site in the Wei River valley of Shaanxi, hold abundant fungi together with damaged starches, which the authors read as cereal alcohol made with a starter of mouldy grain and herbs (qu and caoqu). Some of the fungi resemble Aspergillus and Rhizopus, the moulds common in modern qu. At Lingkou, the second site studied, the drinks were made with sprouted millet instead. The reading rests on the shapes of microscopic remains and is the authors' interpretation.

impact.note: The qu method came to be used across East Asia (reach 2) and a whole line of rice wines, sauces, pastes and vinegars rests on it (generativity 2); depth is held at 1 because these villagers already brewed with malt and the link from this find to the later tradition is the authors' argument.

date.label: between c. 5850 and c. 4950 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: The pottery tested at Guantaoyuan, near the Wei River in Baoji, comes from the site's earliest deposits, of the Baijia Period, 7800 to 6900 cal. BP (about 5850 to 4950 BCE by the 1950 convention).

evidence.supports: Guantaoyuan (GTY hereafter), excavated in the 2000s, is ∼300 km west of LK. It is situated on a high platform in a small basin near the Wei River. The earliest material deposits date to the Baijia Period (7800–6900 cal. BP)

date.label: between c. 5850 and c. 4950 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Far more fungal particles and starches inside those Guantaoyuan vessels than in the soil outside them are read as cereal fermentation with a qu starter; the date is that of the deposits in the first event.

evidence.supports: much higher abundancies of fungal particles associated with ubiquitous starches from residues on vessel interiors than in the sediments on exteriors indicate the presence of cereal-based fermentation using qu as a starter

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Coordinates of Guantaoyuan: the place is given as the Baoji area because no fetched source gave site coordinates; the paper puts the site about 300 km west of Lingkou, in Baoji.
The identification of qu from fungal and starch shapes has not been confirmed by other methods here; independent assessments of the method should be looked for.
The date of the earliest textual reference to qu (the lead cites texts by c. 1000 BCE).
Transmission of qu to Korea and Japan (koji).

unresolved.about: chronology and origin of mould starters
unresolved.note: Older proposed mould-starter brewing in the Lower Yangzi and Huai valleys provides a chronological comparison. Their chronological order, similar vessel shapes and inferred processes do not establish a specific path of transfer.

evidence.supports: Older proposed rice brewing involving mould in an independent site assemblage.
Reports and compares different site assemblages. The proposed geographic pathway remains a hypothesis.

research.note: Liu and colleagues’ 2019 study documented a proposed Guantaoyuan method. Distinct specimen assemblages reported since then include older evidence attributed to mould-starter brewing at Shangshan and Jiahu. The Guantaoyuan method’s origin and transmission remain unresolved.
